reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: A group of disorders of vertebral segmentation, historically termed Jarcho-Levin syndrome, most often autosomal recessive with variants in Notch-pathway genes (DLL3, MESP2, LFNG, HES7) or TBX6
Characterised by multiple vertebral segmentation defects (hemivertebrae, block and butterfly vertebrae) distributed along the spine
Rib anomalies (fusions, bifid or absent ribs) accompany the vertebral defects and shorten the thorax
The combination produces a short trunk with a short neck and short-trunk disproportionate stature, while the limbs are relatively normal
The dominant clinical threat is thoracic insufficiency: a small, poorly compliant thorax that cannot support normal lung growth and ventilation
In DLL3-related disease the spine may show a characteristic 'pebble beach' or generalised vertebral disorganisation on radiographs
Distinguish from spondylothoracic dysostosis, in which symmetric posterior rib fusion gives a 'crab-like' or fan-shaped thorax
reference.pathophysiology: Spondylocostal dysostosis results from disruption of the Notch signalling pathway that drives the segmentation clock during somitogenesis, most commonly through recessive variants in DLL3, MESP2, LFNG or HES7, or from TBX6-related mechanisms. Faulty oscillatory gene expression disturbs the orderly formation and boundary specification of somites, the embryonic precursors of vertebrae and their associated ribs. The result is multiple, often widespread vertebral segmentation and rib anomalies. Because the axial skeleton and thorax form abnormally, chest volume and compliance are reduced, producing thoracic insufficiency and restrictive respiratory disease.
additionalInvestigations: Whole-spine and chest radiographs to characterise vertebral and rib segmentation defects
Molecular genetic testing of the segmentation-pathway genes (DLL3, MESP2, LFNG, HES7, TBX6)
Pulmonary function and thoracic dimension assessment for thoracic insufficiency
Cross-sectional imaging to plan any spinal or thoracic surgery
Screening for associated anomalies (renal, cardiac) given overlap with wider malformation associations
redFlags: Respiratory distress or failure from thoracic insufficiency, especially in infancy
Rapidly progressive scoliosis compromising lung development
Signs of spinal cord involvement or neurological deficit
Recurrent respiratory infections indicating restrictive lung disease
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends chiefly on the severity of thoracic insufficiency: milder cases have good survival with orthopaedic management of the spine, whereas severe early respiratory compromise carries significant mortality. Multidisciplinary respiratory and orthopaedic care is central.
pitfalls: Focusing on the scoliosis while underestimating the life-limiting thoracic insufficiency
Confusing spondylocostal with spondylothoracic dysostosis, which differ in rib pattern and prognosis
Missing associated visceral anomalies by not screening beyond the skeleton
Assuming dominant inheritance when most forms are autosomal recessive, giving incorrect counselling
